- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) and forecast is low, model underestimates true price — adjust upward, especially in early days of the horizon.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.33) and forecast is high, model overestimates — reduce forecast, especially after sharp spikes.
- Model tends to overreact to recent sentiment swings — dampen forecast magnitude if sentiment shifts sharply within 3–5 days.
- In high-sentiment periods, model often fails to capture mean reversion — if price is above 1.5x historical mean, reduce forecast by 15–30% for next 5 days.
- Overshoots after spikes (e.g., > 3x recent high) are common — cap forecast at 2x recent peak unless sentiment confirms continuation.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.00–0.33) and price is trending, model often lags — forecast should be 1–2 days ahead of true price in such cases.
- In low-sentiment environments, model underestimates volatility — increase forecast variance by 10–20% if sentiment remains flat for >7 days.
